name: Defence Satellite Communications

header.one_liner: Military satellite communications — dedicated defence communication satellites (GSAT series), ground terminals, and secure SATCOM links enabling beyond-line-of-sight command and control for Indian Armed Forces; ISRO and DRDO are the primary providers, with growing private-sector participation.
header.maker: ISRO — defence communication satellites (GSAT series); DRDO — secure communication terminals and encryption; BEL — ground segment equipment; private sector (Tata Advanced Systems, Hughes India) — ground terminals

at_a_glance.Technology: Military SATCOM — dedicated and shared defence communication satellites in geostationary and inclined orbits; secure encrypted voice, data, and video links; ground terminals for ships, aircraft, and mobile army units
at_a_glance.Indian_programme: GSAT-7 (Rukmini — Navy, 2013), GSAT-7A (Air Force, 2018), GSAT-7R (planned Navy replacement), ISRO DRRS (Defence Real-time Relay Satellite), GSAT-11/31 (shared military bandwidth)
at_a_glance.Current_status: India operates 2 dedicated military communication satellites (GSAT-7/Rukmini for Navy, GSAT-7A for Air Force) plus shared bandwidth on ISRO GSAT civil satellites; ground terminal network expanding; indigenous capability strong in satellite and ground segment, but some terminal hardware and encryption chips imported.
at_a_glance.Key_indian_players: ISRO (satellite design, launch, operations), DRDO (secure terminals, encryption), BEL (ground segment), Tata Advanced Systems (SATCOM terminals), Hughes India (VSAT terminals)
at_a_glance.Key_foreign_suppliers: Thales Alenia Space (France/Italy — satellite components, historically), L3Harris (US — SATCOM terminals, historically), Hughes (US — VSAT technology, now localised via Hughes India)
at_a_glance.Critical_gap: Ku-band and Ka-band transponder capacity for military use (India has ~2-3 dedicated military SATCOM satellites vs. adversaries' larger constellations); protected anti-jam SATCOM (MILSTAR/AEHF equivalent); high-throughput satellites (HTS) for bandwidth-intensive C4ISR applications.
at_a_glance.Procurement_value: ~₹10,000-15,000 cr across GSAT military satellites, ground terminals, and DRDO secure communication programmes
at_a_glance.Operational_domains: Naval (ship SATCOM — GSAT-7/Rukmini), Air (aircraft SATCOM — GSAT-7A), Land (army mobile terminals, troop connectivity)

what_it_is.prose: Defence satellite communications are the backbone of beyond-line-of-sight (BLOS) command and control, enabling Indian Armed Forces to maintain secure, jam-resistant communications across the vast geographic spread of India's operational theatre — from the northern borders with China and Pakistan to the Indian Ocean Region. India's military SATCOM ecosystem is anchored by ISRO (which designs, launches, and operates the satellites) and DRDO (which develops secure communication terminals and encryption systems). India currently operates two dedicated military communication satellites: GSAT-7 (codenamed 'Rukmini'), launched in 2013 for the Indian Navy, providing UHF and C-band coverage over the Indian Ocean Region; and GSAT-7A, launched in 2018 for the Indian Air Force, providing extended Ku-band coverage for ground-air and air-air communications. A replacement for GSAT-7 (GSAT-7R or similar) is planned. India also shares bandwidth on ISRO's civil GSAT constellation for military use. The ground segment — terminals on warships, aircraft, and mobile army units — is produced by BEL, Tata Advanced Systems, and Hughes India (a localised version of the US VSAT manufacturer). India's key gaps are in protected/anti-jam SATCOM (no Indian equivalent to the US Milstar/AEHF constellation) and high-throughput satellite (HTS) capacity for bandwidth-intensive C4ISR (command, control, communications, computers, intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance) applications. The advent of low-Earth orbit (LEO) mega-constellations (Starlink, OneWeb) has introduced a new dimension — India is considering whether to leverage commercial LEO constellations for military communications (with appropriate security and sovereignty controls).

capability_notes.summary: India operates 2 dedicated military SATCOM satellites (GSAT-7 for Navy, GSAT-7A for Air Force) with ground terminals produced domestically. Protected anti-jam SATCOM and high-throughput capacity are gaps. NavIC provides indigenous positioning but not SATCOM.

import_dependencies.summary: India has strong indigenous SATCOM satellite capability (ISRO) and growing ground terminal production (BEL, Tata). Key dependencies are in specialised transponder hardware, anti-jam technology, and some ground-terminal components.

items.component: Protected anti-jam SATCOM terminals and waveforms
items.note: India lacks a domestic equivalent to US Milstar/AEHF anti-jam SATCOM; DRDO developing but not yet fielded; some terminal components historically imported.
ISRO is developing HTS capabilities but India's military HTS capacity is limited compared to US/Chinese military constellations.
Most terminal hardware is now produced domestically by BEL, Tata, and Hughes India; some specialised RF components and antennas may still be imported.

dimensions.label: Design ownership
dimensions.note: ISRO designs and builds Indian military communication satellites domestically; DRDO develops secure terminals; design ownership is strong.

dimensions.label: Production ownership
dimensions.note: Satellites built and launched by ISRO; ground terminals produced by BEL and Indian private sector; production is largely domestic.

dimensions.label: Critical component sovereignty
dimensions.note: Anti-jam SATCOM capability is a gap; HTS transponder technology limited; most other components are domestic.

dimensions.label: Scale / operational reach
dimensions.note: Only 2 dedicated military SATCOM satellites (vs. adversary constellations with 5-10+); capacity constrained for bandwidth-intensive C4ISR.

dimensions.label: Export potential
dimensions.note: ISRO has launched communication satellites for foreign clients; Indian military SATCOM ground terminals may have export potential to friendly navies.

faq.question: Which satellites provide military communications for India?
faq.answer: India operates two dedicated military communication satellites: GSAT-7 (codenamed 'Rukmini'), launched in 2013 for the Indian Navy, providing UHF and C-band coverage over the Indian Ocean Region; and GSAT-7A, launched in 2018 for the Indian Air Force, providing extended Ku-band coverage. India also shares bandwidth on ISRO's civil GSAT constellation for military use. A replacement for GSAT-7 is planned.

faq.question: Why is India's military SATCOM capacity limited?
faq.answer: India currently operates only 2 dedicated military communication satellites, compared to adversaries who maintain larger constellations. India's military SATCOM capacity is constrained by: (1) limited transponder availability on dedicated military satellites; (2) sharing civil GSAT bandwidth with military requirements; and (3) the absence of a protected/anti-jam SATCOM constellation (equivalent to US Milstar/AEHF). The arrival of high-throughput satellites and potential LEO constellations (OneWeb, Jio-satellite) may expand capacity, but security and sovereignty controls are under development.

faq.question: Could India use Starlink or OneWeb for military communications?
faq.answer: Low-Earth orbit (LEO) mega-constellations like Starlink (SpaceX) and OneWeb offer high-bandwidth, low-latency global coverage. India is evaluating whether to leverage commercial LEO constellations for military communications with appropriate security controls — including encryption, gateway sovereignty, and protected waveforms. OneWeb has regulatory approval to operate in India. However, relying on foreign LEO constellations for military SATCOM raises sovereignty concerns; India's preferred path is likely a hybrid of indigenous dedicated military satellites plus controlled use of commercial constellations.
